questions.q: Per this lesson, what does a Matching Rule define, as distinct from a Duplicate Rule?
options: Matching Rules define what action to take (Alert, Block, Report); Duplicate Rules define how records are compared

Matching Rules define how Salesforce recognizes that two records likely represent the same real-world entity (object, fields, exact/fuzzy comparison); Duplicate Rules define what happens when a match is found
They are two names for the exact same configuration
Matching Rules only apply to custom objects, never to Lead, Contact, or Account
questions.explain: A Matching Rule defines the comparison logic; a Duplicate Rule references one or more Matching Rules and specifies the resulting action (Alert, Block, or Report) and where it applies (UI, API, or both).

questions.q: What common misconception about Salesforce duplicate handling does this lesson explicitly correct?
options: That Salesforce can detect duplicates at all
That Salesforce blocks duplicate records out of the box -- in reality, Matching and Duplicate Rules have to be deliberately activated and tuned
That Duplicate Rules can only be configured by Salesforce support
That Lead, Contact, and Account are the only objects that can ever have duplicates
questions.explain: The lesson states directly that Salesforce does not block duplicates by default -- standard rules exist for Lead/Contact/Account but must be activated, and custom objects typically start with none configured.

questions.q: Why might an org configure a separate phone-based Matching Rule for Accounts in addition to a name-based one?
options: Phone-based matching is required by Salesforce and cannot be disabled
Name-based matching alone can miss real duplicates that share a phone number but have differently-formatted or misspelled names
Phone numbers are the only field Salesforce is capable of comparing
It has no practical benefit and is purely cosmetic
questions.explain: The lesson gives this as a concrete example of why an object can have multiple Duplicate Rules referencing different Matching Rules -- each one catches a different pattern of duplication that another might miss.

questions.q: Why can't Duplicate Rules alone resolve the 2,000 duplicate Leads created by a bulk import six months ago (per the lesson's description of how Duplicate Rules work)?
options: Duplicate Rules only evaluate records as they're created or edited going forward -- they don't retroactively scan records that already exist, so a separate batch tool like Duplicate Jobs is needed
Duplicate Rules can never be applied to Leads
The import would have been automatically reversed by Salesforce
Duplicate Rules only work on Sundays
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes ongoing prevention (Duplicate Rules, forward-looking) from finding existing duplicates (a separate batch activity like Duplicate Jobs), which is exactly why the 2,000 existing records need a different remedy.

questions.q: What caution does this lesson give about marking too many fields as Required at the UI layer?
options: Required fields are always free of downsides and should be maximized everywhere
It can push users to enter junk values just to get past the form, trading one quality problem (missing data) for another (inaccurate data)
Salesforce limits every object to exactly one Required field
Required fields disable all Validation Rules on that object
questions.explain: The lesson warns that over-using Required fields can backfire: users enter placeholder or junk values to satisfy the requirement, which solves completeness at the cost of accuracy.
